html:
The split in the Russian Orthodox Church in the 1650s and 1660s between the state church and the Old Believers, who refused new rites. A church council confirmed the break in 1666 and 1667.

Patriarch Nikon, backed by Tsar Alexis, set out to bring Russian worship in line with the Greek church. He changed the service books and ordered believers to cross themselves with three fingers instead of two. To many Russians this was a betrayal of true faith, since Moscow saw itself as the last pure Orthodox realm after the fall of Constantinople.

The council of 1666 and 1667 deposed Nikon but kept his reforms and cursed those who used the old rites. The state persecuted the Old Believers. Their leader, the priest Avvakum, was burned in 1682, the monks of the Solovetsky monastery held out in a long siege, and some communities burned themselves rather than give in.

Millions kept the old ways, many on the edges of the empire in Siberia and the north. Old Believer families later became leading merchants and industrialists in Russia.
